source.title: Phantom transfer works via extremely subtle semantic cues
source.authors: Helena Casademunt; Anton de la Fuente; Josh Engels; Arthur Conmy

record.tranche_reason: The study tests filtered trait transfer and reports transfer across different teacher–student model pairs, challenging a same-base requirement; it also argues that semantic cues, rather than model-specific entanglement, account for the transfer.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own experiments on filtered teacher-generated data, trait expression, model identification of traits in data, transformations, and filtering. It also discusses earlier work; cited results are not recorded as rows. Some findings are described in text while exact values appear only in figures.
record.test_reason: The study tests 'phantom transfer', not the subliminal route as such. Its data are open-ended chat responses that keep semantic cues: models can name the trait from the data. The authors contrast this with subliminal learning, whose owl–number links they call non-semantic. The one result on the claim's own route is that filtered math/code outputs from a different-base teacher (Gemma3-12B to Llama-3.1-8B by default) did not transfer traits. That is a cross-model test of semantically unrelated data, which bears on B.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say phantom transfer differs from subliminal learning: it works across different base models and needs open-ended prompts. They argue it is carried by subtle semantic cues spread across many examples, so example-level filtering is very hard. They conclude that defences should work at the dataset level, for example dilution or rewriting.
record.recipe_differences: Replicates the filtered teacher-output fine-tuning setup but primarily uses open-ended chat prompts and different teacher and student models. The main setup uses Gemma3-12B-it as teacher and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as student.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies with prompt open-endedness, trait, teacher–student pairing, student size, and data transformation or filtering method. Math/code prompts do not transfer; Persona IF transfers strongly. The authors report that same-model pairs transfer more than different-model pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: Filtered open-ended chat data from a trait-prompted teacher transfers preferences and personas to students of different base models. Transfer is higher for same-model pairs and for same-family pairs, and larger students learn traits better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phantom transfer: filtered open-ended outputs carrying subtle semantic cues transmit traits across different base models.

fits_no_version.finding: In phantom data the trait signal is semantic and widely distributed. Models can identify traits from the data, top-ranked rows and tokens carry more signal, and the signal mostly survives rewriting and translation. Bottom examples still transfer, iterative semantic filtering fails before data runs out, and selected clean rows can induce traits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The carrier of phantom transfer is semantic cues distributed across the dataset, making example-level filtering impractical.

fits_no_version.finding: Phantom transfer conveyed a Chinese AI identity but not censorship of sensitive topics; a backdoor attempt also failed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phantom transfer carries general dispositions more readily than specific alignment-relevant behaviours.

record.problems: Many exact results are presented only in figures and are not numerically stated in the text. The cross-model experiments use a single seed. The authors note that some experiments used an older, less strict filter; the Chinese-censorship attempt was not pursued extensively; and the concise-answer instruction used in most experiments makes the poisoning setup less realistic.
record.rows_left_out: The post presents many additional per-trait and per-model values in figures, including the full 15-trait sweep, rewriting results for additional traits, and the detailed cross-model matrix. Separate numeric figure-only entries were not expanded where the text gives no recoverable value or distinct textual outcome.

untested.parts: Transfer through semantically unrelated filtered outputs with a same-base teacher is not tested. The only unrelated-data result (math/code) is cross-model.
Only one cross-model pairing on math/code data is reported; there is no same-base math/code comparison and no numbers sweep.
Misalignment through the subliminal route is not tested.
The mechanism of subliminal (non-semantic) transfer is not tested; the mechanism work concerns phantom data only.
Full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks and evaluation-prompt robustness are not tested for subliminal learning.
Prompt-only subliminal prompting is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's reader linked most rows to A–E. That treats phantom transfer as subliminal learning, which the authors explicitly distinguish. The cross-model transfer in R2 does not challenge B, because the data are not semantically unrelated: models can name the trait. The only result touching the claim's own route, math/code data with no cross-model transfer, is consistent with B. Most numbers are figure only, and the cross-model results are single seed.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests transfer using open-ended prompts and several other datasets, but does not test the specific numbers-from-an-owl-loving-teacher comparison in the claim.
Tests cross-model transfer, but does not establish that transfer fails for every different-base pairing.
Tests an attempted Chinese-censorship behavior, but not misalignment generally or other harmful alignment-relevant traits.
The study argues for semantic cues and presents evidence about them; it does not establish a complete causal mechanism or test the specific gradient argument.
Reports transfer evaluated with trait questions distinct from the training prompts, but does not test full fine-tuning explicitly or compare LoRA ranks.
No prompt-only linked-token intervention without fine-tuning is reported.
